The reproductive biology of the cardinalfish Epigonus crassicaudus remains relatively poorly documented, but recent work has begun to clarify key milestones. At a stable water temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C], a temperature typical of its deep shelf and upper slope habitat, the species shows a notably slow pace of life. Hatching from the small, pelagic eggs yields lecithotrophic larvae that weigh only 0.000113 grams [Wwb = 0.000113 grams] at birth, a value derived from an egg diameter of just 0.6 millimeters reported for the congeneric Epigonus affinis. This extremely low wet weight at birth reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo, a common pattern among marine teleosts that produce numerous, small pelagic eggs. The initial larval phase is therefore characterized by a rapid depletion of endogenous yolk, and the onset of first exogenous feeding must occur within a narrow window after mouth opening and yolk-sac resorption to avoid the point of no return.

Growth proceeds very gradually in this species, and individuals do not attain sexual maturity until they reach a standard length of approximately 20 centimeters [Lp = approximately 20 centimeters]. This length at puberty is a critical life-history threshold; it represents the point at which gonad maturation begins and the HPG axis becomes fully activated. Given the cold, stable thermal regime at 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C], which slows metabolic and developmental processes, the transition to the sexually mature adult stage requires several years of sustained feeding. The fish continue to grow slowly after reaching maturity, and field surveys indicate that the ultimate standard length, or the maximum size an individual can achieve, is 43 centimeters [Li = 43 centimeters]. This asymptotic size is not commonly observed, as the vast majority of specimens captured are considerably smaller, suggesting that only a few individuals survive long enough to attain this upper limit under natural conditions.

As individuals approach their ultimate size, they also approach their maximum body mass. The ultimate wet weight of the species, based on a length-weight relationship fitted to a large sample of specimens, is 874 grams [Wwi = 874 grams]. Achieving this mass, which corresponds to the fully grown, reproductively viable organism, requires both an extended growth period and access to adequate prey resources. The length-weight relationship, described by the equation reported in the supplementary material, shows that body mass scales with length with an exponent of nearly three, indicating roughly isometric growth. Interestingly, a comparison with other members of the Epigonidae family reveals that this asymptotic mass is modest relative to the maximum standard length of 43 centimeters [Li = 43 centimeters], suggesting a somewhat slender body plan typical of benthopelagic foragers. The body shape may be an adaptation for efficient cruising in the water column above the continental slope.

At the stable temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C] that defines their environment, the life span of Epigonus crassicaudus is remarkably extended. The oldest documented individuals reach an age of approximately 54 years [am = approximately 54 years], a longevity that places this species among the more long-lived member at a temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C]s of its genus. This figure is derived from the analysis of otolith growth increments, which corroborate the slow annual growth rates inferred from length-frequency data. The extreme longevity at such a low ambient temperature is consistent with the metabolic theory of ecology, which predicts that cold-water organisms have slower rates of senescence. It is notable that while 54 years [am = 54 years] represents the maximum recorded longevity, the median life span is likely considerably shorter due to natural mortality from predation and the energetic demands of reproduction at a temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C]. Nonetheless, the potential for such extended survival underscores a life-history strategy based on delayed reproduction and high adult survival.

Females of Epigonus crassicaudus are iteroparous and produce multiple batches of eggs each year. At the prevailing temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C], the annual reproductive output amounts to approximately 90,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 90,000 eggs per year], a rate that reflects a high fecundity typical of broadcast spawners. The relatively high reproductive rate, coupled with the extremely small size of the newly hatched larvae, recorded at 0.000113 grams [Wwb = 0.000113 grams], is among the lowest documented for teleosts of comparable adult size, reflecting an extreme fecundity-driven strategy. This stands in contrast to species that produce fewer, larger eggs with greater yolk reserves. The combination of small egg size, a long life span of 54 years [am = 54 years], and delayed maturity at a length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters] paints a picture of a species that relies on high fecundity and iteroparity to persist in a stable but resource-limited deep-sea environment at a temperature of 7.5 °C [T = 7.5 °C].
